record.paper_title: Enabling and Emerging Technologies for Social Distancing: A Comprehensive Survey and Open Problems
record.context_brief: pandemic mode for phones and infrastructure
record.original_question: How can future smartphone and smart-infrastructure designs implement a pandemic mode that uses infected-movement data to set regional risk levels and automatically configures sensors and wireless connections such as cellular, Bluetooth, and Wi-Fi for contact tracing, while helping users avoid contagious diseases and practice social distancing?

evidence.quote: An occasional pandemic outbreak in a particular period can drive the mobile service providers, e.g., Google and Apple, to build up a pandemic mode application for current users’ mobile devices, e.g. smartphones.

Then, based on the current infected movement data, e.g., the current reported number of infected people and currently infected areas, from the government officials, the service providers can determine the risk levels of the pandemic and activate a certain level in the smartphones.

In particular, if the authorities activate low-risk levels, i.e., the current number of infected people and areas are small, the smartphones can trace close contacts using cellular networks only. In this case, the pandemic mode application will disable certain sensors, Bluetooth, and Wi-Fi by default. However, if high-risk level pandemic mode, i.e., the current number of infected people and areas are large, is activated, the pandemic mode application will enable all of the wireless connections including Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, and cellular network, as well as relevant sensors automatically to trace contacts faster.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Design a "pandemic mode" framework for smartphones and smart infrastructure with the following specifications, and analyze its feasibility and effectiveness:

1. Inputs. A continuously updated dataset D(t) of infected-movement information at time t, consisting of (a) the reported number N(t) of currently infected individuals and (b) a collection A(t) of geographic regions currently flagged as infected, both supplied by public-health authorities.

2. Risk classification. Define a risk-level function R: D(t) → {L_1, L_2, …, L_k} (with at least a low-risk and a high-risk level) that maps the current infection data to a discrete regional risk level for each region r ∈ A(t), based on thresholds applied to N(t) and the size/density of A(t).

3. Device configuration policy. Specify a policy π that, given the risk level R(r,t) of the region r in which a device is located, automatically configures the device's sensors and wireless interfaces (cellular, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi) for contact tracing such that:
   • At a low risk level, only the cellular network is used for contact tracing, and Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, and non-essential sensors are disabled by default to conserve energy and preserve privacy.
   • At a high risk level, all wireless interfaces (cellular, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi) and the relevant sensors are enabled simultaneously to provide faster and finer-grained contact tracing.
   • Intermediate levels interpolate between these two extremes.

4. User-facing functionality. The system must additionally provide each user with alerts and route/location guidance enabling them to avoid contagious individuals and maintain social-distancing constraints (a minimum spatial separation d_min from other users).

The problem is to (i) give a precise mathematical specification of R and π (including thresholds, transition rules, and triggering conditions), (ii) prove or argue that the resulting policy minimizes a suitable joint cost combining tracing latency, energy consumption, and infection-exposure probability, and (iii) describe the supporting smart-infrastructure architecture that allows seamless coordination between devices, base stations, and the public-health authority's data feed.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is a forward-looking system-design open problem rather than a precisely stated mathematical conjecture. Aspects related to it (privacy-preserving Bluetooth-based contact tracing such as Google/Apple Exposure Notifications, multi-modal contact-tracing schemes, and risk-adaptive sensing) have been partially developed since 2020, but no complete, formally specified and provably optimal "pandemic mode" framework that automatically reconfigures sensors and cellular/Bluetooth/Wi-Fi interfaces according to authority-issued regional risk levels appears to have been established. The problem therefore remains open in its full generality.

status_evidence.title: Privacy-Preserving Contact Tracing (Apple/Google)
status_evidence.snippet: Apple and Google partnered on Exposure Notifications using Bluetooth for contact tracing.
status_evidence.claim: Partial industry deployment addresses some aspects, but not adaptive risk-level-driven multi-radio reconfiguration.
